results.summary: This design encodes amateur radio WSPR messages from a callsign, locator and power level into 162 symbols and generates corresponding sine and cosine PWM outputs for 4-FSK transmission. It is configured over a 115200 baud UART using a provided Python script, and a start_transmission input triggers the symbol sequence. The PWM outputs require external low-pass filtering, and the I/Q signals are intended to work with the TinyWhisper analog project on the same shuttle. Silicon testing confirmed that UART configuration and transmission start work and that 25% duty cycle local oscillator and PWM data appear on the outputs, though the RF output itself was not validated.

This project implements a Turing machine with a configurable state transition table on a single Tiny Tapeout tile. It supports manual and automatic modes, tape initialization, wrap and loop options, and bank selection, with status and tape contents shown on external LED and 7-segment displays. Control is via DIP switches and pushbuttons for clock and reset, allowing step-by-step configuration and execution. The design is intended as an educational demonstration of Turing machine operation and requires external LED PMODs, a 7-segment display, and switches for full use.

This design renders an analog-style clock on a VGA monitor, using a CORDIC algorithm to compute hand angles and pixel positions. It includes an alarm function that compares a set alarm time to the current time and outputs a 3.15 kHz square wave pulsed at 1 Hz for a buzzer. Time and alarm settings are adjusted via five external pushbuttons, and the VGA output follows the standard Tiny Tapeout VGA PMOD pinout. The design requires a 31.5 MHz clock and external pushbuttons with pulldown resistors, and the alarm output needs an external driver for a buzzer.

This is a 4-bit saturating counter with a seven-segment display output, written in VHDL. The counting direction is controlled by input pin 0, and the counter saturates at 15 when counting up and at 0 when counting down. The seven-segment output is active-low with the decimal point as the most significant bit. Testing requires an external clock and a seven-segment display; no other external hardware is specified.

This project implements a minimal 8-bit CPU with a simple datapath and two finite-state machines. It accepts serial input data through the ui_in pins and provides an 8-bit output along with carry, zero, overflow, and negative flags. A start signal triggers serial input, and multiplexer select lines control internal routing. No external hardware is required for operation.

This design is a third-order digital FIR filter with an 8-bit architecture, configurable cutoff frequency, and selectable low-pass or high-pass behavior. It accepts 8-bit data input and provides 8-bit filtered output, with configuration pins for weight selection, filter type, and enable. The documentation is minimal, providing only the pinout and a one-line description, so details of the filter coefficients and testing procedure are not available.

This is a logic game where the player must convert a decimal number shown on a seven-segment display into its binary equivalent using eight DIP switches before a timer expires. The design uses a 1 kHz clock and provides seven-segment display outputs for the decimal number and game status. Input is via the eight DIP switches, and the game logic includes a timer to create pressure. No external hardware beyond the DIP switches and a seven-segment display is required.

This design implements a Turing machine in Turing's original mathematical construction, using external SPI ROM and RAM for the transition table and tape. It supports 128 states and an alphabet size of 256, with separate SPI interfaces for state and tape memory. The design is difficult to test because it requires preloading the external memory devices with data before execution. It requires one 512Kbit ROM and one 512Kbit RAM, and the ROM can be emulated by the on-board RP2040.

This is a test project synthesized with Dyno-SV, a new open-source synthesis tool, to gate level using the SkyWater 130nm standard cell library. The design finds the indices of the first, second, and third set bits in an 8-bit input word and outputs their positions along with valid flags. It also includes a counter and configuration bits to select registered or combinational input and output paths. The project serves as a validation of the Dyno-SV synthesis flow and requires no external hardware.

This project implements an 8-bit successive-approximation-register (SAR) ADC in an analog process, converting an analog input voltage to an 8-bit digital output. It includes a sample-and-hold circuit, a comparator, and a digital SAR logic block, with enable and calibration inputs for the comparator. The design currently lacks full rail-to-rail detection without precise timing and accurately converts only above approximately 0.8V; it requires two clock signals, one for the digital logic and a slower one for sampling. External hardware such as a signal generator and oscilloscope is needed for testing.
